title: Civics Questions and Answers (2008 version)
stop: The officer asks up to 10 questions; 6 correct passes.
who: For applicants who filed Form N-400 before October 20, 2025.

senior.text: Applicants 65 or older who have been lawful permanent residents for 20 or more years may study just the 20 questions marked with an asterisk (*). The officer asks 10 of them, and 6 correct passes. They may take the civics test in the language of their choice.

intro: The 100 civics (history and government) questions and answers for the naturalization test are listed below. The civics test is an oral test and the USCIS Officer will ask the applicant up to 10 of the 100 civics questions. An applicant must answer 6 out of 10 questions correctly to pass the civics portion of the naturalization test.

parts.title: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information

method: Transcribed word for word from two independent copies (A and B in sources), compared by script; every difference was settled by a third look and is listed under "resolved". Straight quotes were set as typographic quotes.

questions.q: What is the supreme law of the land?
questions.idea: The Constitution is the highest law in the country. Every other law, federal or state, must agree with it, and a law that goes against it can be struck down by the courts. Article VI calls it “the supreme Law of the Land.” Memory hook: the Constitution sits at the top of the ladder of laws.

questions.q: What does the Constitution do?
questions.idea: The Constitution sets up the government, defines its three branches and their powers, and protects the basic rights of Americans. It was written in 1787 and took effect in 1789. Any one of the three answers is correct.

questions.q: The idea of self-government is in the first three words of the Constitution. What are these words?
questions.idea: “We the People” are the first three words of the Constitution. They show that the government’s power comes from the people, not from a king. This is the idea of self-government, also called popular sovereignty.

questions.q: What is an amendment?
questions.idea: An amendment is a change or addition to the Constitution. It is usually proposed by two-thirds of both houses of Congress and ratified by three-fourths of the states. The word comes from “amend,” which means to improve or correct.

questions.q: What do we call the first ten amendments to the Constitution?
questions.idea: The first ten amendments are called the Bill of Rights. They were added in 1791 to protect basic rights, such as freedom of speech and religion and the right to a fair trial. Many states agreed to the Constitution only after being promised these protections.

questions.q: What is one right or freedom from the First Amendment?
questions.idea: The First Amendment protects five freedoms: speech, religion, assembly (gathering peacefully), press and petition (asking the government to fix a problem). Memory hook: “RAPPS,” religion, assembly, press, petition, speech.

questions.q: How many amendments does the Constitution have?
questions.idea: The Constitution has 27 amendments, or changes. The first ten, the Bill of Rights, were added together in 1791. The most recent, the 27th, took effect in 1992 and is about pay raises for members of Congress. Amending is hard on purpose, so it has happened only 27 times in more than 230 years.

questions.q: What did the Declaration of Independence do?
a: said that the United States is free (from Great Britain)
questions.idea: The Declaration of Independence was adopted on July 4, 1776. It told the world that the thirteen colonies were now free and independent states, no longer ruled by Great Britain. It also gave the reasons: people have rights, and a government that destroys those rights loses its claim to rule.

questions.q: What are two rights in the Declaration of Independence?
questions.idea: The Declaration of Independence names “Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness” as rights that every person has. It calls them unalienable, meaning no government gives them and none may take them away. Name any two.

questions.q: What is freedom of religion?
a: You can practice any religion, or not practice a religion.
questions.idea: Freedom of religion means you may follow any religion, or none at all, and the government may not force a religion on you. It comes from the First Amendment, which forbids Congress to set up an official religion or stop people from practicing their faith.

questions.q: What is the economic system in the United States?
questions.idea: The United States has a capitalist, or market, economy. Most businesses are privately owned, and prices are set mostly by buying and selling. Government still makes some rules, such as laws about safety and fair dealing.

questions.q: What is the “rule of law”?
a: No one is above the law.
questions.idea: The rule of law means the same laws apply to everyone, including the people who make and enforce them. Leaders cannot simply do what they want; they must follow the law like anyone else. Memory hook: “No one is above the law.”

questions.q: Name one branch or part of the government.
questions.idea: The government has three branches: legislative (Congress), executive (the President) and judicial (the courts). Any one of the six answers names a branch. Memory hook: Congress makes the laws, the President carries them out, the courts explain them.

questions.q: What stops one branch of government from becoming too powerful?
questions.idea: Checks and balances let each branch limit the others. For example, the President can veto a bill, Congress can override a veto, and courts can strike down laws that break the Constitution. Separating powers among three branches keeps any one from becoming too powerful.

questions.q: Who is in charge of the executive branch?
questions.idea: The President is in charge of the executive branch, which carries out the laws. The branch includes the Vice President, the Cabinet and the federal departments and agencies.

questions.q: Who makes federal laws?
questions.idea: Congress, the legislative branch, makes federal laws. It has two parts, the Senate and the House of Representatives, and a bill must pass both. Article I of the Constitution gives Congress this power.

questions.q: What are the two parts of the U.S. Congress?
questions.idea: Congress has two parts, or “houses”: the Senate and the House of Representatives. A bill must pass both before it goes to the President. This two-house design is called a bicameral legislature. It came from the Great Compromise of 1787.

questions.q: How many U.S. Senators are there?
questions.idea: Each of the 50 states has two senators, so there are 100 in all. Every state gets the same number, no matter how many people live there. Memory hook: 50 states × 2 = 100.

questions.q: We elect a U.S. Senator for how many years?
questions.idea: Senators serve six-year terms. The terms are staggered: about one third of the Senate is elected every two years. The long term lets senators take a longer view, and the staggering means the whole Senate never changes at once.

questions.q: Who is one of your state’s U.S. Senators now?
a: Answers will vary. [District of Columbia residents and residents of U.S. territories should answer that D.C. (or the territory where the applicant lives) has no U.S. Senators.]
questions.idea: This answer depends on where you live, and it changes after elections. To find your two senators, go to senate.gov and choose your state, or see USCIS’s page uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates. Give the name of a senator serving on the day of your interview. People in Washington, D.C., and the U.S. territories have no U.S. senators, and saying so is the right answer for them.

questions.q: The House of Representatives has how many voting members?
questions.idea: The House of Representatives has 435 voting members. Congress fixed that number by law, and it has stayed at 435 for most of the time since 1913. Seats are divided among the states by population, so big states have many representatives and small states may have only one. Washington, D.C., and the territories send delegates who cannot vote on the final passage of bills.

questions.q: We elect a U.S. Representative for how many years?
questions.idea: Members of the House serve two-year terms, so every seat is on the ballot every even-numbered year. The short term keeps representatives close to the voters, who can quickly keep them or replace them.

questions.q: Name your U.S. Representative.
a: Answers will vary. [Residents of territories with nonvoting Delegates or Resident Commissioners may provide the name of that Delegate or Commissioner. Also acceptable is any statement that the territory has no (voting) Representatives in Congress.]
questions.idea: This answer depends on your address, and it changes after elections. Go to house.gov and use “Find Your Representative” with your ZIP code, or see uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates. Give the name of the person serving on the day of your interview. People in territories with a nonvoting delegate or resident commissioner may name that person.

questions.q: Who does a U.S. Senator represent?
questions.idea: A U.S. senator represents all the people of his or her state, not just one district. That is why each senator must think about the whole state.

questions.q: Why do some states have more Representatives than other states?
questions.idea: Seats in the House are shared out by population. After each census, taken every ten years, the seats are divided again, so states that grow can gain seats and others can lose them. This is called apportionment. The Senate is different: every state has two senators.

questions.q: We elect a President for how many years?
questions.idea: The President is elected for a four-year term. Presidential elections are held every four years, in years that can be divided by four, like 2024 and 2028. Since the 22nd Amendment, a President can be elected only twice.

questions.q: In what month do we vote for President?
questions.idea: Presidential elections are held in November, every four years. By law, Election Day is the Tuesday after the first Monday in November. The new President takes office the next January 20.

questions.q: What is the name of the President of the United States now?
a: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the name of the President of the United States.
questions.idea: This answer changes with elections, so this page does not print a name. USCIS keeps the current answer at uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates; check it shortly before your interview. Give the name of the person who is President on the day of your interview. The President is elected every four years and takes office on January 20.

questions.q: What is the name of the Vice President of the United States now?
a: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the name of the Vice President of the United States.
questions.idea: This answer changes with elections, so this page does not print a name. USCIS keeps the current answer at uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates; check it before your interview. The Vice President is elected together with the President, on the same ticket, and also serves as President of the Senate.

questions.q: If the President can no longer serve, who becomes President?
questions.idea: If the President dies, resigns or is removed from office, the Vice President becomes President. The 25th Amendment, added in 1967, made this rule clear. This has happened nine times in American history.

questions.q: If both the President and the Vice President can no longer serve, who becomes President?
questions.idea: If both the President and the Vice President can no longer serve, the Speaker of the House becomes President. This order is set by a law, the Presidential Succession Act of 1947. After the Speaker come the President pro tempore of the Senate and then members of the Cabinet.

questions.q: Who is the Commander in Chief of the military?
questions.idea: The Constitution makes the President the Commander in Chief of the Army and Navy, which today means all the armed forces. This puts the military under the control of an elected civilian. Congress still holds the power to declare war and to pay for the military.

questions.q: Who signs bills to become laws?
questions.idea: After both houses of Congress pass a bill, it goes to the President. If the President signs it, it becomes law. This is one of the checks between the branches: Congress writes the law, and the President must agree, or Congress must override a veto.

questions.q: Who vetoes bills?
questions.idea: A veto is the President’s refusal to sign a bill. The word is Latin for “I forbid.” Congress can still make the bill a law if two-thirds of the House and two-thirds of the Senate vote to override the veto. This is a clear example of checks and balances.

questions.q: What does the President’s Cabinet do?
questions.idea: The Cabinet is the group of top advisers to the President, mostly the heads of the big executive departments, such as the Secretary of State and the Attorney General. They advise the President and run their departments. The Constitution mentions the heads of departments giving their opinions in writing; the custom of meeting as a Cabinet began with George Washington.

questions.q: What are two Cabinet-level positions?
a: Secretary of Health and Human Services
Secretary of Housing and Urban Development
questions.idea: The Cabinet includes the Vice President and the heads of the executive departments, such as the Secretary of State, the Secretary of Defense and the Attorney General. Memorize two that are easy for you to say. Most titles begin with “Secretary of”; the head of the Justice Department is called the Attorney General.

questions.q: What does the judicial branch do?
a: decides if a law goes against the Constitution
questions.idea: The judicial branch, the courts, reviews and explains laws and settles disagreements about them. It can also decide whether a law goes against the Constitution. This power is called judicial review, confirmed in Marbury v. Madison in 1803.

questions.q: What is the highest court in the United States?
questions.idea: The Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States. It is the only court the Constitution names; Congress created the lower federal courts. Its decisions on the Constitution and federal law are final for all other courts. It meets in Washington, D.C.

questions.q: How many justices are on the Supreme Court?
a: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the number of justices on the Supreme Court.
questions.idea: USCIS lists this answer at uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates, because the number is set by law, not by the Constitution, and Congress could change it. Check that page before your interview. The number has stayed the same since 1869.

questions.q: Who is the Chief Justice of the United States now?
a: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the name of the Chief Justice of the United States.
questions.idea: This answer changes when a new Chief Justice is appointed, so this page does not print a name. USCIS keeps the current answer at uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates. The Chief Justice leads the Supreme Court and is chosen by the President with the approval of the Senate. Like the other justices, the Chief Justice serves for life.

questions.q: Under our Constitution, some powers belong to the federal government. What is one power of the federal government?
questions.idea: Some powers belong only to the national government, so the country acts as one. It prints money, declares war, creates an army and makes treaties with other countries. The Constitution lists these powers in Article I, and Article I, Section 10, forbids the states to do them.

questions.q: Under our Constitution, some powers belong to the states. What is one power of the states?
questions.idea: Powers not given to the national government belong to the states or the people (the 10th Amendment). States provide schools, police and fire protection, give driver’s licenses and decide how land may be used. Name any one.

questions.q: Who is the Governor of your state now?
a: Answers will vary. [District of Columbia residents should answer that D.C. does not have a Governor.]
questions.idea: This answer depends on your state, and it changes after elections. Look on your state’s official website, or see uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates, which points to official sources. The governor is the head of the executive branch of a state, much as the President is for the nation. Washington, D.C., has no governor; it has a mayor, and saying D.C. has no governor is the right answer there.

questions.q: What is the capital of your state?
a: Answers will vary. [District of Columbia residents should answer that D.C. is not a state and does not have a capital. Residents of U.S. territories should name the capital of the territory.]
questions.idea: This answer depends on where you live. Learn the capital city of your state; your state’s official website lists it. The capital is where the state legislature meets and the governor works. People in D.C. answer that D.C. is not a state; people in a territory name its capital.

questions.q: What are the two major political parties in the United States?
questions.idea: The two major political parties today are the Democratic Party and the Republican Party. Most elected officials belong to one of them. The Republican Party was founded in the 1850s, and the Democratic Party traces its roots to the 1820s and earlier. Other, smaller parties also exist.

questions.q: What is the political party of the President now?
a: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the political party of the President.
questions.idea: This answer changes with elections, so this page does not print it. USCIS keeps the current answer at uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates; check it shortly before your interview. Give the party of the person who is President on the day of your interview.

questions.q: What is the name of the Speaker of the House of Representatives now?
a: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the name of the Speaker of the House of Representatives.
questions.idea: This answer can change whenever the House chooses a new Speaker, so this page does not print a name. USCIS keeps the current answer at uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates. The Speaker is elected by the House to lead it and is next in line for the presidency after the Vice President.

questions.q: There are four amendments to the Constitution about who can vote. Describe one of them.
a: You don’t have to pay (a poll tax) to vote.
Any citizen can vote. (Women and men can vote.)
A male citizen of any race (can vote).
questions.idea: Four amendments widened the right to vote. The 15th (1870) says the vote cannot be denied because of race, and the 19th (1920) says it cannot be denied because of sex. The 24th (1964) ended poll taxes in federal elections. The 26th (1971) lowered the voting age to 18. Each official answer describes one of these.

questions.q: What is one responsibility that is only for United States citizens?
questions.idea: Only citizens may serve on a jury and vote in federal elections. These are responsibilities as well as rights: juries depend on citizens to decide cases fairly, and elections depend on citizens to choose leaders. Name either one.

questions.q: Name one right only for United States citizens.
questions.idea: Only U.S. citizens may vote in federal elections and run for federal office. These rights let citizens choose their leaders and become leaders themselves.

questions.q: What are two rights of everyone living in the United States?
questions.idea: Many rights protect everyone in the United States, citizen or not: freedom of speech and expression, freedom of assembly, freedom to petition the government, freedom of religion and the right to bear arms. Most come from the First and Second Amendments. Name any two.

questions.q: What do we show loyalty to when we say the Pledge of Allegiance?
questions.idea: When you say the Pledge of Allegiance, you promise loyalty to the flag and to “the Republic for which it stands,” the United States. The first version was written in 1892 by Francis Bellamy, and Congress made it official in 1942. Saying it is a choice; no one can be forced to say it.

questions.q: What is one promise you make when you become a United States citizen?
a: give up loyalty to other countries
defend the Constitution and laws of the United States
obey the laws of the United States
serve in the U.S. military (if needed)
serve (do important work for) the nation (if needed)
be loyal to the United States
questions.idea: New citizens take the Oath of Allegiance at the naturalization ceremony. They promise to give up loyalty to other countries, defend the Constitution and laws, obey the laws, be loyal to the United States, and serve the nation, in the military or otherwise, if needed. Name any one.

questions.q: How old do citizens have to be to vote for President?
questions.idea: Citizens must be 18 or older to vote for President. The 26th Amendment set the voting age at 18 in 1971. Before then most states required voters to be 21.

questions.q: What are two ways that Americans can participate in their democracy?
a: give an elected official your opinion on an issue
publicly support or oppose an issue or policy
questions.idea: Americans take part in their democracy in many ways: voting, joining a political party or civic group, helping with a campaign, contacting their senators and representatives, speaking out on issues, writing to a newspaper or running for office. Name any two.

questions.q: When is the last day you can send in federal income tax forms?
questions.idea: Federal income tax forms are usually due on April 15. When April 15 falls on a weekend or holiday, the deadline moves to the next business day. Taxes pay for the work of the federal government.

questions.q: When must all men register for the Selective Service?
questions.idea: Men must register with the Selective Service at age 18, and the law covers men from 18 until they turn 26. The list would be used to draft soldiers fairly if Congress ever brought back the draft. There has been no draft since 1973.

questions.q: What is one reason colonists came to America?
questions.idea: People came to the colonies for many reasons. Some, like the Pilgrims and Puritans, wanted to worship in their own way. Others wanted land, work or a chance to get ahead. Some were escaping persecution or hard times at home. Memory hook: “faith, freedom and fortune.”

questions.q: Who lived in America before the Europeans arrived?
questions.idea: American Indians, also called Native Americans, lived across North America for thousands of years before Europeans arrived. They formed hundreds of nations with their own languages, governments and ways of life, from the pueblos of the Southwest to the Iroquois Confederacy in the Northeast.

questions.q: What group of people was taken to America and sold as slaves?
questions.idea: Millions of Africans were captured, taken across the Atlantic Ocean and sold as slaves in the Americas. About 400,000 of them were brought to the land that became the United States. The first enslaved Africans in English Virginia arrived in 1619. Slavery lasted in the United States until the 13th Amendment ended it in 1865.

questions.q: Why did the colonists fight the British?
a: because of high taxes (taxation without representation)
because the British army stayed in their houses (boarding, quartering)
questions.idea: The colonists fought the British mainly because Parliament taxed them though they had no representatives there: “taxation without representation.” They were also angry that British soldiers were quartered, or housed, in their homes, and that they were losing the right to govern themselves.

questions.q: Who wrote the Declaration of Independence?
questions.idea: Thomas Jefferson of Virginia wrote the first draft of the Declaration of Independence in June 1776, when he was 33. A committee that included John Adams and Benjamin Franklin helped, and Congress edited the text before adopting it. Jefferson later became the third President.

questions.q: When was the Declaration of Independence adopted?
questions.idea: The Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776, in Philadelphia. That is why Independence Day is July 4. Congress had voted for independence two days earlier, on July 2, and then approved the final words on the 4th.

questions.q: There were 13 original states. Name three.
questions.idea: The 13 original states were the 13 British colonies on the Atlantic coast: New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia. Memory hook: pick three you can say easily, such as New York, Virginia and Georgia.

questions.q: What happened at the Constitutional Convention?
a: The Founding Fathers wrote the Constitution.
questions.idea: At the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia in 1787, delegates from twelve states wrote the Constitution. They met to fix the weak Articles of Confederation and instead wrote a whole new plan of government. George Washington presided.

questions.q: When was the Constitution written?
questions.idea: The Constitution was written in 1787 at the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia. It was signed on September 17, 1787, and took effect in 1789 after enough states ratified it. Memory hook: Declaration 1776, Constitution 1787.

questions.q: The Federalist Papers supported the passage of the U.S. Constitution. Name one of the writers.
questions.idea: The Federalist Papers were 85 essays written in 1787 and 1788 to persuade New Yorkers to ratify the new Constitution. Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay wrote them, and they signed every essay with the same pen name, “Publius.” Any of the four names is an accepted answer.

questions.q: What is one thing Benjamin Franklin is famous for?
a: oldest member of the Constitutional Convention
first Postmaster General of the United States
questions.idea: Benjamin Franklin was a printer, scientist, writer and diplomat. He published “Poor Richard’s Almanac,” became the first Postmaster General, helped start an early lending library in Philadelphia and, at 81, was the oldest member of the Constitutional Convention. As a diplomat in France, he won French help in the Revolution.

questions.q: Who is the “Father of Our Country”?
questions.idea: George Washington is called the “Father of Our Country.” He led the Continental Army to victory in the Revolution, presided over the Constitutional Convention and became the first President. His example of stepping down after two terms shaped the presidency.

questions.q: Who was the first President?
questions.idea: George Washington was the first President, serving from 1789 to 1797. He won every electoral vote, twice. Many of the customs of the presidency, such as the Cabinet and the two-term tradition, began with him.

questions.q: What territory did the United States buy from France in 1803?
questions.idea: In 1803 the United States bought the Louisiana Territory from France for about $15 million. It was a huge area west of the Mississippi River, and it roughly doubled the size of the country. President Thomas Jefferson then sent Lewis and Clark to explore it.

questions.q: Name one war fought by the United States in the 1800s.
questions.idea: The United States fought four wars on the list in the 1800s: the War of 1812 with Britain, the Mexican-American War (1846–1848), the Civil War (1861–1865) and the Spanish-American War (1898). Memory hook: one war with Britain, one with Mexico, one at home, one with Spain.

questions.q: Name the U.S. war between the North and the South.
questions.idea: The Civil War (1861–1865) was fought between the Union in the North and the Confederacy in the South; it is sometimes called the War between the States. The Union won, the nation stayed together, and slavery was ended.

questions.q: Name one problem that led to the Civil War.
questions.idea: Slavery was the central issue that led to the Civil War. Arguments about states’ rights and the economy were tied to it; for example, the Southern states’ declarations of secession pointed to the protection of slavery. All three answers are accepted.

questions.q: What was one important thing that Abraham Lincoln did?
a: led the United States during the Civil War
questions.idea: Abraham Lincoln, the 16th President, led the country through the Civil War and preserved the Union. He issued the Emancipation Proclamation, which declared enslaved people in the rebelling states free. He was assassinated in April 1865.

questions.q: What did the Emancipation Proclamation do?
a: freed slaves in the Confederate states
freed slaves in most Southern states
questions.idea: President Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation on January 1, 1863, during the Civil War. It declared enslaved people free in the states that were fighting against the Union. It did not free enslaved people in border states that stayed loyal; the 13th Amendment (1865) ended slavery everywhere in the country.

questions.q: What did Susan B. Anthony do?
questions.idea: Susan B. Anthony was a leader of the movement for women’s rights in the 1800s, especially the right to vote. She also worked against slavery. She was arrested for voting in 1872. The 19th Amendment, which gave women the vote in 1920, is sometimes called the Susan B. Anthony Amendment.

questions.q: Name one war fought by the United States in the 1900s.
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: The United States fought in five wars on this list in the 1900s: World War I (1917–1918), World War II (1941–1945), the Korean War (1950–1953), the Vietnam War, and the Persian Gulf War (1991). Any one of them is a correct answer.

questions.q: Who was President during World War I?
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: Woodrow Wilson was President during World War I. He asked Congress to declare war on Germany in 1917. After the war he proposed the League of Nations to keep the peace.

questions.q: Who was President during the Great Depression and World War II?
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: Franklin D. Roosevelt was President from 1933 to 1945, through most of the Great Depression and most of World War II. He is the only President elected four times. After him, the 22nd Amendment limited Presidents to two elected terms.

questions.q: Who did the United States fight in World War II?
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: In World War II, the United States and its allies fought the Axis Powers: Japan, Germany and Italy. Memory hook: “JGI,” Japan, Germany, Italy. Japan’s attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941 brought the United States into the war.

questions.q: Before he was President, Eisenhower was a general. What war was he in?
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: Before he became the 34th President, Dwight D. Eisenhower was a general in World War II. He was the supreme commander of the Allied forces in Europe, and he led the D-Day landings in 1944.

questions.q: During the Cold War, what was the main concern of the United States?
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: During the Cold War, the main concern of the United States was communism, especially its spread by the Soviet Union. The U.S. policy of trying to stop communism from spreading was called containment. The Cold War lasted from the late 1940s to 1991.

questions.q: What movement tried to end racial discrimination?
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: The civil rights movement worked to end racial discrimination and segregation. Through court cases, peaceful protests, boycotts and marches, it won major laws in the 1960s, such as the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

questions.q: What did Martin Luther King, Jr. do?
a: worked for equality for all Americans
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: Martin Luther King, Jr. was a minister who led the civil rights movement with peaceful, nonviolent protest. He worked for equal rights for all Americans. His “I Have a Dream” speech (1963) is one of the most famous in American history, and a national holiday honors him.

questions.q: What major event happened on September 11, 2001, in the United States?
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: On September 11, 2001, terrorists took over four passenger planes. Two hit the World Trade Center in New York City, one hit the Pentagon near Washington, D.C., and one crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after passengers fought back. Nearly 3,000 people were killed. It was the deadliest attack on American soil in the nation’s history.

questions.q: Name one American Indian tribe in the United States.
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.note: [USCIS Officers will be supplied with a list of federally recognized American Indian tribes.]
questions.idea: There are hundreds of American Indian tribes in the United States; the federal government recognizes more than 570 of them as nations with their own governments. Any tribe on the list is an accepted answer. Pick one name you can say with confidence, such as Cherokee, Navajo or Sioux. The list includes broad groups too, such as the Iroquois, a confederacy of six nations, and the Arawak of the Caribbean.

questions.q: Name one of the two longest rivers in the United States.
questions.idea: The Missouri and the Mississippi are the two longest rivers in the United States, each a little over 2,300 miles long. The Missouri flows into the Mississippi near St. Louis, and the Mississippi flows south to the Gulf near New Orleans. Name either one.

questions.q: What ocean is on the West Coast of the United States?
questions.idea: The Pacific Ocean is on the West Coast, where California, Oregon and Washington meet the sea. Memory hook: West = Pacific, East = Atlantic.

questions.q: What ocean is on the East Coast of the United States?
questions.idea: The Atlantic Ocean is on the East Coast, where the 13 original colonies were founded. Settlers from Europe crossed the Atlantic to reach America.

questions.q: Name one U.S. territory.
questions.idea: The United States has five territories where people live year-round: Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa, the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam. They are part of the United States but are not states. Name any one.

questions.q: Name one state that borders Canada.
questions.idea: Thirteen states border Canada, from Maine in the east to Washington in the west, plus Alaska. Pick one easy name, such as New York, Michigan or Washington.

questions.q: Name one state that borders Mexico.
questions.idea: Four states border Mexico: California, Arizona, New Mexico and Texas. Memory hook: they run along the southern border from the Pacific to the Gulf.

questions.q: What is the capital of the United States?
questions.idea: Washington, D.C., is the capital of the United States. “D.C.” stands for District of Columbia, a federal district that is not part of any state. The Constitution allowed for such a district, and the government moved there in 1800. The city is named for George Washington.

questions.q: Where is the Statue of Liberty?
a: Liberty Island [Also acceptable are New Jersey, near New York City, and on the Hudson (River).]
questions.idea: The Statue of Liberty stands on Liberty Island in New York Harbor, close to the New Jersey shore; that is why New Jersey and the Hudson River are also accepted. It was a gift from the people of France and was dedicated in 1886. For millions of immigrants arriving by ship, it was one of the first sights of America.

questions.q: Why does the flag have 13 stripes?
a: because the stripes represent the original colonies
questions.idea: The flag has 13 stripes, 7 red and 6 white, for the 13 original colonies that became the first states. Memory hook: the stripes look back to the beginning; the stars count the states today.

questions.q: Why does the flag have 50 stars?
a: because there is one star for each state
because each star represents a state
questions.idea: The flag has 50 stars, one for each state. A new star is added on the Fourth of July after a state joins. The 50-star flag has flown since July 4, 1960, after Hawaii became the 50th state.

questions.q: What is the name of the national anthem?
questions.idea: The national anthem is “The Star-Spangled Banner.” Francis Scott Key wrote the words in 1814 after watching the British attack Fort McHenry in Baltimore during the War of 1812. In the morning he saw the American flag still flying. Congress made it the national anthem in 1931.

questions.q: When do we celebrate Independence Day?
questions.idea: Independence Day is celebrated on July 4. It marks the day in 1776 when the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence. It is the country’s birthday, celebrated with parades and fireworks.

questions.q: Name two national U.S. holidays.
questions.idea: There are eleven federal holidays: New Year’s Day, Martin Luther King, Jr. Day, Presidents’ Day, Memorial Day, Juneteenth, Independence Day, Labor Day, Columbus Day, Veterans Day, Thanksgiving and Christmas. Juneteenth, the newest, marks June 19, 1865, when news of freedom reached enslaved people in Galveston, Texas. Name any two.
